How to curate

Untick whatever is a false positive, then use the buttons to export a FASTA of the approved EVEs only, run the hierarchical clustering or draw the genomic-context figures. Candidates found by the HMM alone appear in group 5_HMM_ONLY and can be selected like any other. The selection lives in curation_selection.json and does not alter the pipeline tables. Synteny is optional: tick the box before clustering across species, or use the synteny column in the species TSV to control it row by row. Rows marked review hit a viral target whose genome type is unknown in RefSeq: decide them here like any other row. Every chart follows the approved EVEs and the manual family/protein, and the page refreshes itself when the data on disk changes.

Overview of the approved EVEs

Viral families shared between species

How to read it · UpSet plot

Each viral family of the approved EVEs (manual family edits included) is counted once per species that carries it. The bars on the left give the number of families in each species. Each column is one exact combination of species, the filled dots under it: its bar counts the families found in those species and in no other one, so every family sits in exactly one column. A column with a single dot holds families only that species has; a column with every dot holds the families all species share. Hover a column or a species for the family names and their EVE counts. EVEs without a family are left out.

Evidence per segment

How it works · what it means

Click a slice or a bar to filter the table. "HMM domain only" are the segments with no alignment that only the HMM supports. CD-Search is the conserved-domain search on CDD (local rpsblast+ by default); its domains are placed in a scope from their CDD description and source taxon, and only RNA virus and ssDNA virus (non-retroviral) count as in scope — reverse transcriptases, integrases, gag and pararetroviruses are kept apart. Pfam (hmmscan on Pfam-A with the Pfam gathering thresholds) uses the same scopes; every source is drawn on the ORF under inspect.

Accumulation along the chromosome

Sequence features of the approved EVEs

EVE length

ORF length (nt), per species; log-scale axis.

EVE %GC

GC content of the ORF; the diamond marks the host genome GC.

ΔGC EVE − genome

EVE GC minus the mean host genome GC (percentage points).

ΔGC flank − EVE

GC around the EVE (10, 25 and 50 kb each side, EVE excluded) minus the EVE GC.

Viral proteins and domains

Inner ring: protein class (manual edits included). Outer ring: with an HMM viral domain or not.

Taxonomy of the best viral hit

Repeats and low complexity around the EVEs

How it works · what it means

Each approved EVE locus (overlapping ORFs of one insertion together) gets three checks. Low complexity: dustmasker on the EVE sequence and segmasker on its peptide; a candidate mostly masked (≥ 50%) is probably a compositional artefact, not a viral fragment. Soft-masking: NCBI assemblies write repeats in lower case, so the masked share of the EVE and of each flank is compared with the whole genome. Transposons nearby: the ORFs of the flanks (six frames, ≥ 100 aa) are searched with the transposon domains of Pfam-A (gathering cut-offs) and grouped into LTR retrotransposon (integrase, gag, protease), retrotransposon RT, non-LTR endonuclease, DNA transposon and Helitron. Each locus then reads low complexity, inside TE (a TE domain overlaps the EVE, or it is mostly masked), TE nearby (a TE domain within the flank), repeat-rich flank (flanks masked well above the genome), clean, or short flanks when the contig leaves nothing to judge. Non-retroviral EVEs often sit next to retrotransposons, whose reverse transcriptase may have copied the viral RNA into DNA. Runs on segments use the whole genomes of synteny_genomes.tsv.

EVEs on the viral proteins

How it works · what it means

Each approved EVE realigned (Smith-Waterman, BLOSUM62) on a viral reference protein, the grey bar. With shared, the EVEs of one family go on the protein most of them hit in the DIAMOND search, so the fragments of one gene line up; * marks the EVEs whose own best hit is that protein. Each row is a genomic-context cluster, so the pieces of one broken gene share a row. Hatched bars align on the opposite strand or in another frame than the ORF (blastx found the viral signal there), so the ORF itself is probably not the viral reading frame. Every approved ORF is drawn, also the overlapping ones hidden by "one row per locus". Click a bar to inspect the EVE.

Flow of the approved EVEs

Sequence viewer

How to read a card

One card per EVE locus (the overlapping ORFs of one insertion together, shown through their representative ORF). The header carries the viral family and protein, the length, the verdict and the read evidence of every library mapped on the page: DNA = libraries where the insertion is present / libraries with data; RNA = RNA-seq libraries with ≥ 5 reads inside the locus; sRNA = small RNA reads and the strongest piRNA signature (● ping-pong, ▲ primary 5′U, ▼ A10 only). Opening a card reads the locus from the server: verdict, the genomic context with every read track, the domain architecture, the reads library by library, the tblastn segments and the clusters it belongs to, and its sequence. Curating (qualify / reject, family, protein) stays in Inspection: the button at the end of each card opens it.

Reads over the EVEs

Genomic DNA is the insertion in the genome of each library: fixed, polymorphic or absent

Presence in the DNA libraries

How it works · what it means

Each row is an approved EVE locus, each column a DNA library (the assembly reads first, then the individuals and pools by population). The call is the one of the Genomic DNA tab, with its thresholds: present = the EVE is covered and its depth matches the flanks; het = present, with reads of a chromosome without the insertion as well (reads clipped at the junction); partial = only part of the EVE covered or its depth well below the flanks; absent = no read on the EVE while the flanks are covered; excess = much deeper than the flanks or the genome (a repeat, or a copy elsewhere landing here); no data = the flanks have too few reads to say. A fixed insertion is present in every individual; a polymorphic one in some. Libraries mapped elsewhere (a cluster) enter with their measurements only. Hover a cell for its numbers; click a row to open its card.

RNA-seq transcription of each EVE, library by library

Transcription in the RNA-seq libraries

How it works · what it means

Reads of every RNA-seq BAM of the species (short reads, long reads, Iso-Seq) counted over each approved locus: reads inside the EVE have aligned bases in it (a read whose splice gap only jumps over the EVE is not counted), mean depth is averaged over the locus, share covered is the fraction with at least one read. The colour is on a log scale, one hue, darker = more; empty = no read. For a stranded library the hover gives the depth on each genome strand. A transcribed EVE is not proof of a functional gene: read-through from a host gene or a nearby transposon transcribes it as well — the card shows whether the reads continue into the flanks.

Small RNA siRNA and piRNA over each EVE: primary (5′ U), secondary (A10) and the ping-pong cycle

Small RNA reads

piRNA calls:
How it works · what it means

Small RNA reads mapped with the sRNAProfiler method (Bowtie1, at most one mismatch); a read placed at N sites counts 1/N at each, and a read belongs to an EVE when at least half of it falls inside. The cell colour is the abundance (log scale); the glyph is the piRNA signature of the piRNA-sized reads (24–31 nt), read strand by strand: ▲ primary — one strand carries a 5′ uridine bias (5′ U at or above the threshold), the mark of primary piRNAs cut from long precursor transcripts (piRNA clusters); EVE-derived primary piRNAs are usually antisense to the viral ORF. ▼ secondary — an adenine at position 10 (A10) on a strand, the mark of secondary piRNAs, without a significant ping-pong overlap. ● ping-pong — the 5′ ends of piRNAs on opposite strands overlap by exactly 10 nt more often than by any other distance (z-score of the 10-nt overlap against 1–20 nt, sRNAProfiler); with a 5′ U strand and an A10 strand facing each other this is the ping-pong amplification cycle: the primary piRNA guides the cleavage of a complementary transcript, whose fragment becomes the secondary piRNA. ◆ siRNA — sRNAProfiler calls the locus siRNA (20–22 nt, both strands, no ping-pong). The thresholds above change the calls at once; the table under the heatmap lists every locus with enough piRNA-sized reads, strand by strand (sense / antisense = relative to the EVE's ORF).

Actions


      

    

    

      
Read mapping — small and long RNA

      
How it works · what it means
Reads mapped here show under every map of the page
        (an EVE under inspect, an expanded context cluster, an expanded tblastn segment), so transcription and small RNA
        production can be weighed when deciding whether an EVE is real.

        Small RNA follows sRNAProfiler.
        Give the reads with the adapters already removed: they are mapped on the whole genome with Bowtie1 allowing at most
        one mismatch (-v 1 -k 20 --best --strata), and a read placed at N positions counts 1/N at each.
        For every span the reads with at least half their length inside it give its size profile (18–35 nt), strand, 5′ U,
        A at position 10, the 10-nt ping-pong overlap and the class of sRNAProfiler's rule set (siRNA 20–22 nt on both strands;
        piRNA 24–31 nt with 5′ U or ping-pong). An optional Bowtie index of rRNA/tRNA drops structural RNA first.

        Long and other RNA follow ViralQuest:
        minimap2 -ax <preset> | samtools sort, and the coverage track is its track — bar height is depth, bar colour is
        the mean base quality, + strand above and − strand below for stranded libraries, with mean depth, breadth, CV and mean
        quality. minimap2 -ax sr does not open introns: a short read crossing one is clipped at the junction.

        Mapping runs in the background, one file at a time; BAMs made elsewhere can be added as they are.

      

        
        

      

      

      

    

    

      
Online BLASTX (NCBI)

      
How it works · what it means
Sends the genome sequence of the chosen segments to NCBI BLASTX in batches of at most
        20 sequences and 10,000 nt (longer segments are split into overlapping windows). Each batch keeps
        its RID on disk, so the run survives a closed page or a restarted server: press Resume.
        Segments already searched with the same database and E-value come from the cache.
        The NCBI queue can take from minutes to hours.

      

        
        
        
        
      

      
      
      

        
        
        
      

      

      

    

  

  

    

      
Genomic-context clusters

        
        
        
        
        
  
        
        
        
        
      

      
How it works · what it means
Approved EVEs grouped by where they sit in the genome.
        A segment is one locus (overlapping reading frames count once); segments on the same
        contig closer than the distance above form a cluster. A singleton is a cluster of
        one segment. The cluster names come from the pipeline (eve_hits_diretos.merged.bed);
        rejecting an EVE removes it here, so a pipeline cluster can turn into a singleton.
        remove on a cluster or on one of its segments rejects those EVEs everywhere (candidate table,
        charts, exports): they leave this table for the Removed box under it, where restore brings
        them back.

      

      

        

        

      

      

        
        
        
        
        
      

      

      

    

    

      
Distance between EVEs

        
        
        
        
      

      

    

    

      
Distance to the nearest EVE, per species

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      

      
How it works · what it means
How far apart are the EVEs in the genome, and is
        there a pattern? For every approved EVE locus (the overlapping ORFs of one insertion together) the distance to the
        nearest other approved locus of the same genome: the gap between them, edge to edge (0 when they touch). It is
        measured on the original chromosome or contig — a run made on extracted segments is placed back on the whole genome
        first — so a locus alone on its contig has no neighbour and is counted apart. Each ridge is one species: the density
        of the gaps on a log scale, with one tick per EVE under it and a dot at the median. The dashed line is the same
        number of EVEs, with the same lengths, dropped at random on the assembly (a contig drawn in proportion to its
        length, a uniform position on it) 200 times and measured the same way; the hollow dot is its median.
        Closer than random: the observed median gap is smaller than in at least 95% of the random genomes
        (pclustered ≤ 0.05) — EVEs come in groups: pieces of one viral genome integrated together, tandem copies,
        or hotspots such as piRNA clusters. More spread than random is the opposite. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov D compares
        the whole distributions. The null ignores what the genome is made of (repeats, gaps, heterochromatin), and a very
        fragmented assembly leaves most EVEs without a neighbour on their contig: read those species with care.

      

      

      

    

  

  

    

      
tblastn scan of the viral references

        
        
        
  
        
        
        
        
        
      

      
How it works · what it means
The best viral hit of every ORF kept by the DIAMOND
        screening is aligned back on the whole genome with tblastn (six frames, no ORF needed), so
        viral stretches broken by stops or frameshifts show up too. HSPs closer than the distance above
        form a segment; every orfipy ORF inside it is listed, the candidates and the ORFs never
        analysed (new), with their screening result and their CD-Search and Pfam domains.
        The ORFs come from the scan's own distance: to characterise the ORFs between HSPs that only a
        larger distance joins, run the scan again with that distance. Expand a segment for its map and alignments.
        remove drops a segment from the scan, the bridges and the exports and rejects its candidates in the
        candidate table too; it then waits in the Removed box under the table, where restore brings back
        the segment and the candidates that left with it.

      

        
        
        
        
      

      

      

        
        
        
        
        
      

      

      

    

  

  

  

    
EVE clusters shared between species

      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
    

    
How it works · what it means
The approved EVEs of every
      species are aligned all-vs-all with tblastx and clustered in two stages (pairs above the identity and
      coverage of the run become edges; each group is then split at the valleys of its distance distribution).
      A cluster with segments of two or more species is shared, but only a pair of segments of
      different species that align well (identity and coverage above the values here) says the
      insertion may be the same — an orthologous EVE or a very close viral source. Shared clusters without
      such a pair are distant: the same viral family, not the same insertion, and they stay out unless
      show distant is ticked. Species and clusters are ordered by average-linkage trees over which
      clusters each species carries (Jaccard), so species with the same EVEs sit side by side. Click a
      cluster for the tblastx identity and coverage of every pair of its segments, ordered by their
      distance (1 − bitscore of the pair / bitscore of the self-hit).


      Units: the comparison can use each approved ORF, each genomic-context cluster or each tblastn segment,
      the last two merged at the distance chosen here. Flank synteny: for every locus of a shared cluster the
      flanks are read from its genome and their host genes are labelled with DIAMOND blastx against the reference
      proteome. A pair of loci of different species is syntenic when they share neighbour genes on both
      sides (either orientation), one side when only one side matches, not syntenic when both have
      neighbours and none is shared, and insufficient when a flank has no labelled gene (short contig).
      Syntenic loci are probably one ancestral insertion; not syntenic ones, independent integrations.
      Genes found next to more distinct sites than max sites in one species, and mobile elements, are
      ignored. Runs made on pre-extracted segments use the whole genomes listed in
      synteny_genomes.tsv in the results folder.

Host genes hit by the candidates

      
How it works · what it means
The peptide of every candidate is searched against
        reference host proteomes (DIAMOND blastp, best hit per ORF in each proteome; isoforms of a gene are collapsed).
        The table lists the host genes that were hit, with the candidates that hit each one. A host gene is not always a non-EVE:
        an old insertion is often annotated as a gene of the host, and some cellular genes are hard to tell from viral ones — so
        nothing is removed here by the page. You remove the genes you judge to be real host genes: removing a gene rejects
        every candidate ORF that hit it (the whole locus, as everywhere else), and restoring the gene brings them back.

        Flags: uncharacterised — the gene has no described function, so it may be the EVE itself annotated as a gene;
        same species — the hit is in the proteome of the candidate's own species at ≥ 95 % identity, i.e. that genome
        annotation simply contains this ORF; host ≥ viral — the host hit scores at least as much as the best viral hit.

        Removed host genes (TSV) is the list to report in the methods: each gene removed by hand with the ORFs it took.
        It is also written to 13_curadoria/host_genes/removed_host_genes.tsv when the selection is saved.

      

        

        

          
          

      

    

    

      
Genes

        
        

      

        
        
        
        
        
        

      

      

    

  

  

    

      
Genomic DNA reads — integration and presence across samples

      
How it works · what it means
DNA reads are mapped on the whole genome
        (minimap2 -ax sr, or map-ont / map-pb / map-hifi), so no read is forced onto an EVE;
        only the alignments over the EVE loci ± 5 kb are kept, so a whole-genome BAM is never written.

        Assembly reads (the DNA the genome was assembled from) show whether the insertion is really in the genome: an integrated EVE
        is covered like its flanks and like the rest of the genome, and reads cross both EVE/host junctions. A depth far above the genome
        points to an exogenous virus or a contaminant; a junction no read crosses points to a chimeric contig.

        Population reads (other individuals, or pools) show where the EVE is present. For an individual the cell is
        present / partial / absent; for a pool it is the estimated frequency, EVE depth over flank depth. Reads aligned on the
        flank and clipped exactly at the junction ("empty site") come from chromosomes without the insertion.

        Only the measurements are stored. The calls are made here, with the thresholds below, and change as you move them.
        "No data" means the flanks themselves are not covered: that is low coverage, not absence.

      

        
        
        

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        

      

      

    

    

      
Loci × samples

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      

      

      

    

  

  

  

    
Circulating virus sequences

      

    
How it works · what it means
Add the coding sequences
      (CDS) of circulating viruses, in nucleotides and in frame from their first base; every approved EVE is then
      measured on the same features. The family of each CDS comes from its header: the NCBI Virus custom definition
      line (acc |title|molecule type|species|genus|family|length, the same fields as the RefSeq viral
      proteins of the tool, chosen under Download → Coding region → Build custom), a family=… tag,
      or any word ending in -viridae. A sequence without one takes the family typed here or, when ticked, the
      family of its best DIAMOND blastp hit on the viral database of the run. Each CDS is translated and searched with
      the same calibrated viral HMMs that annotate the EVEs, so with domain means the same on both sides.
      Host genes (for example datasets download genome accession GCF_… --include cds) are a reference
      for the host's own composition, drawn in grey: an EVE that drifted from its family towards them has been
      ameliorated by the host genome. A CDS with internal stops is kept but flagged: it usually means a wrong frame or
      an annotation problem.

    

      
      
      
      
      
      
    

    
    

    
Host genes from the genome annotation

    
The CDS of every annotated host gene (longest isoform) are read from the genome with its GFF3 or GTF:
      genes within the neighbour window of an EVE become host near EVEs, a sample of the rest host genome.
      The GFF is the one set here, the third column of synteny_genomes.tsv, the run's own (whole-genome
      runs), or a GFF next to the genome FASTA with the same name or accession. Runs on segments are placed on the whole
      genomes of synteny_genomes.tsv.

    

  

  

    
Composition analysis

      
      
      
      
    

    
How it works · what it means
EVEs in the viral frame.
      Each approved EVE locus is read in the frame of its viral protein: the stretch DIAMOND aligned (blastx
      qseq) translated in the frame that aligns best to the reference protein of the protein map. The ORF
      frame is not used, because in many EVEs the longest ORF is another frame of the insertion and its codons say
      nothing about the virus. One locus is one point (the longest stretch among its overlapping ORFs); EVEs found by
      the HMM alone have no aligned viral protein and stay out unless ticked below.


      Features. Composition (%GC, GC1, GC2, GC3, GC12, GC3s at the synonymous third positions), codon usage
      (RSCU of the 59 codons of amino acids with synonyms; ENC, Wright 1990) and dinucleotide odds ratios
      ρ = f(XY) / f(X)·f(Y) over the whole sequence and at codon positions 1-2, 2-3 and 3-1 (across two codons),
      written with U for T. ρ below 0.78 is under-represented, above 1.23 over-represented. Short stretches give noisy
      codon usage: ENC and RSCU need about 100 codons to settle, the dinucleotides fewer; min. codons trades
      EVEs kept for precision.


      Best discriminators. Each feature is ranked by its Kruskal–Wallis H across the groups chosen (groups with
      at least 3 sequences); a feature correlated (|r| > 0.9) with one already chosen is skipped. Ranking on the
      circulating viruses alone (the default) leaves the EVEs out of the choice, so where they fall in the PCA is not
      built in; ranking by EVE vs circulating picks the features that changed after integration, and a PCA on them
      will always separate the two. PCA on z-scores; with fit on circulating the axes come from the
      circulating viruses and the EVEs are projected onto them. t-SNE (scikit-learn, fixed seed) on the same
      z-scores keeps neighbours, not distances: the gaps between its clusters mean little. Sets are capped per virus
      species so a heavily sequenced virus does not dominate; host sets are subsampled.

Feature by group

      
      
      
      
    

    

    

  

  

    
EVEs between their virus and their host genes

      
      
      
      
    

    
How it works · what it means
After integration an EVE is no longer
      a virus: it mutates as host DNA, and its composition drifts from that of its viral family towards that of the
      host genome around it (amelioration). Each EVE is placed on the axis that goes from the centroid of the
      circulating viruses of its family (0) to the centroid of the host genes (1):
      A = (EVE − virus)·(host − virus) / |host − virus|², in z-scores. The host end is either the genes within the
      neighbour window of that EVE (its local genomic context) or the host genome sample. A near 0 = it still looks
      like the virus (recent, or under constraint); near 1 = it looks like its host genes (old, or in a region of
      strong mutational bias); below 0 or above 1 = beyond either end. It is a projection: noise of a short EVE off
      the axis does not pull it towards 0.5. An EVE needs at least 3 circulating CDS of its family to be placed.
      Below, EVE by EVE: one feature at a time, the band is the interquartile range of the circulating viruses
      of the family (line at the median), ● the EVE, ▲ the mean of its neighbouring genes on a light bar from their
      lowest to their highest value, and the host genome mean (a dotted line, or ■ per EVE when the family has EVEs
      in several species). Click an EVE to link it to its neighbouring genes in the PCA and the t-SNE.

    

    
EVE by EVE

      
      
      
      
      
    

    

    

  

  

    
Codon usage

      
      

    

      
ENC plot
ENC against GC3s. The dotted curve is the ENC expected when only the
        GC mutational bias shapes the codons (Wright 1990); points well below it are shaped by something else
        (selection, or a host that the EVE now follows).

      
Neutrality plot
GC12 against GC3 (Sueoka 1988). A slope near 1 means mutation
        pressure sets the composition; near 0, selection on the protein. Lines: least squares per origin.

        

    

    

  

  

    
Relative synonymous codon usage

      

    
Mean RSCU per group. 1 = the codon is used as often as its synonyms; red under-used, blue over-used
      (above 1.6 or below 0.6 is usually called a preference). Codons are grouped by amino acid.

    

  

  

    
Dinucleotide odds ratios

      
      

    
Mean ρ per group (U = T). Red under-represented (ρ < 0.78), blue over-represented (ρ > 1.23).
      CpG and UpA at positions 2-3 and 3-1 are the classic marks of RNA viruses mimicking their hosts; position 3-1
      is the freest from the protein sequence.

PLANCUS · quick guide

    
From the pipeline results to a curated EVE catalogue, on one page.
      Every chart and table reads the same data: the candidates and your decisions.

    
Suggested workflow

    
    
      
  1. Pipeline — see where each number on this page comes from.
    2. 
      
  2. Inspection — filter and sort the candidate table; inspect opens one EVE in its own tab
        (position, neighbours, GC, domains, alignments, primers, long and small RNA reads) ending with Approve / Reject.
        The decision lands back here automatically.
    3. 
      
  3. Save — the save button on top writes the curation to 13_curadoria/.
        A save • mark means there are unsaved decisions.
    4. 
      
  4. Re-analyse and export — approved EVEs feed the FASTA exports, clustering, genomic-context
        figures, repeats, tblastn scan and the cross-species comparison; each runs from its tab.
    5. 
    

    
Tabs

    
Overview charts of the approved set · Inspection candidate table and curation ·
      Clusters genomic loci and hierarchical clustering · tblastn genome segments recovered by the final scan ·
      Cross-species shared clusters, heatmap and flank synteny · Circulating viruses GC, codon usage and
      dinucleotides of the EVEs next to circulating virus CDS you add, with PCA and t-SNE.
